questions.q: Which of the following system services does the Jack OS implement?
choices: Memory management (objects, arrays)
I/O device drivers
A file system
Multi-tasking
Networking
Security
questions.explain: Of the system services, the Jack OS implements only memory management and I/O device drivers. A file system, UI management (shell/windows), multi-tasking, networking and security are all left out.

questions.q: Which of the following does the Jack OS provide as language extensions (as opposed to system services)?
choices: Mathematical operations such as abs and sqrt
Abstract data types such as String and Array
Graphics output such as drawLine and drawCircle
Memory management
I/O device drivers
questions.explain: The language extensions are math operations, abstract data types (String, Array), input functions, textual output and graphics output. Memory management and I/O drivers count as system services.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the eight Jack OS classes?
choices: Sys
Keyboard
Array
Process
questions.explain: The eight classes are Math, Memory, Screen, Output, Keyboard, String, Array and Sys. There is no process class, since the Jack OS has no multi-tasking.

questions.q: A Jack program reads two side lengths and prints the hypotenuse, using a helper function Main.hypot. Which of these calls are OS services?
choices: Keyboard.readInt(...)
Output.printString(...)
Math.sqrt((x*x) + (y*y))
Main.hypot(a, b)
questions.explain: Keyboard, Output and Math are OS classes. Main.hypot is a function the program defines itself.

questions.q: On the Hack platform, OS functions run in a special protected mode and get more hardware resources than user-level code.
questions.explain: OS code is privileged on typical computers, but on Hack the OS code and user-level code are treated exactly the same way.

questions.q: On typical (non-Hack) computers, OS code is considered privileged. What does that involve?
choices: Accessing OS services requires a permission mechanism more elaborate than a simple function call
OS functions execute in a special protected mode
OS functions receive more hardware resources
OS functions must be written directly in machine language
questions.explain: Privileged OS code means an elaborate permission mechanism, a protected execution mode and extra hardware resources. Nothing requires OS code to be written in machine language. The Jack OS, for example, is written in Jack.

questions.q: You want to implement an existing OS made of n highly inter-dependent modules, and you have executable versions of all n. What strategy do the slides recommend?
choices: Implement each module separately, using the remaining n-1 executable modules to support it
Implement all n modules first, then test them together
Implement modules strictly in dependency order, starting with the module that depends on nothing
Replace the other n-1 modules with empty stubs while developing each one
questions.explain: This reverse-engineering strategy lets you build and test each module in isolation, with the other modules fully working. The slides note that many versions of Unix were developed this way.

questions.q: The naive multiply(x, y) adds x to a running sum y times. Its running time is proportional to:
choices: The value of y
The number of bits in y (log2 y)
The number of 1-bits in y
A constant, independent of y
questions.explain: Repeated addition loops y times, so the work grows with the value of y itself, which can be up to about 32767 on Hack.

questions.q: The long multiplication algorithm loops over the bits of y, adding a shifted copy of x whenever the bit is 1. Its running time is proportional to:
choices: The number of digits (bits) in y, i.e. log2 y
The value of y
The value of x * y
The square of the value of y
questions.explain: The loop runs once per bit, so the cost grows with log2 y. Because the word length is fixed (16 bits), this is effectively O(1).

questions.q: Trace long multiplication on multiply(27, 9). Which values of xShifted get added to sum?
questions.explain: 9 = 1001 in binary. xShifted takes the values 27, 54, 108, 216 for i = 0..3. Only bits 0 and 3 are 1, so sum = 27 + 216 = 243.

questions.q: When long multiplication computes multiply(x, 11), how many times does it execute sum = sum + xShifted?
questions.explain: 11 = 1011 in binary, which has three 1-bits. The addition happens only on iterations where the i'th bit of y is 1. xShifted is doubled on every iteration regardless.

questions.q: If x and y are two's complement values, the long multiplication algorithm works as-is, with no special handling for negative inputs.
questions.explain: The slides state that the algorithm works as-is for two's complement inputs. Division, by contrast, divides |x| by |y| and then sets the sign.

questions.q: If the true product x*y does not fit in n bits, what does the long multiplication algorithm return?
choices: The correct answer modulo 2^n
Zero
An error code via Sys.error
The largest representable n-bit value
questions.explain: Overflowed bits are simply lost, so the result is always correct modulo 2^n.

questions.q: To implement the helper bit(x, i), the slides suggest a static array twoToThe in class Math, built in Math.init. What is twoToThe[10]?
questions.explain: twoToThe[i] = 2^i for i = 0..15, so twoToThe[10] = 1024. ANDing x with twoToThe[i] tells you whether bit i is set, without any bit shifting.

questions.q: The multiplication and division algorithms use O(N) additions, and each addition takes O(N) operations, for O(N^2) overall. Why is this still essentially O(1) on Hack?
choices: N, the number of bits, is fixed at 16
Hack performs every addition in zero time
The algorithms skip all zero bits, so they run in constant time
The results are cached in the twoToThe array
questions.explain: N is the word size, which is fixed at 16, so the work is bounded by a constant. Asymptotically faster algorithms exist, but they only pay off when the number of bits is very large.

questions.q: The naive divide(x, y) repeatedly subtracts y and counts how many subtractions it does. Its running time is proportional to:
choices: The value of x (more precisely x / y)
log2 x
The number of 1-bits in y
A constant
questions.explain: Repeated subtraction loops once per unit of the quotient, so for small y the run time grows with the value of x. Long division, and the recursive algorithm, run in time proportional to log2 x.

questions.q: The recursive algorithm is: if (y > x) return 0; q = divide(x, 2*y); if ((x - 2*q*y) < y) return 2*q else return 2*q + 1. For divide(175, 3), the inner call divide(175, 6) returns 29. What does divide(175, 3) return?
choices: 2*q = 58, because 175 - 2*29*3 = 1 is less than 3
2*q + 1 = 59, because 175 - 2*29*3 = 1 is less than 3
2*q + 1 = 59, because 175 - 2*29*3 = 1 is positive
2*q = 58, because 29 is odd
questions.explain: x - 2*q*y = 175 - 174 = 1. That leftover is less than y = 3, so there is no room for another y, and the result is 2*q = 58 (remainder 1).

questions.q: Using the same recursive algorithm, divide(45, 4) makes the call divide(45, 8), which returns 5. What does divide(45, 4) return?
questions.explain: q = 5, and x - 2*q*y = 45 - 40 = 5. That is not less than y = 4, so one more y fits and the result is 2*q + 1 = 11.

questions.q: The recursive divide keeps doubling y, which can overflow. How is this detected and handled?
choices: Overflow makes y negative, so the first statement becomes: if (y > x) or (y < 0) return 0
Overflow makes x negative, so the function returns x
Sys.error is called whenever 2*y exceeds 32767
The recursion depth is capped at 16 calls
questions.explain: Doubling a large positive 16-bit value wraps it to a negative number. Checking y < 0 alongside y > x ends the recursion correctly.

questions.q: How does the division implementation handle signed (possibly negative) inputs?
choices: Divide |x| by |y|, then set the quotient's sign
It works as-is on two's complement values
It returns 0 for any negative input
It converts both inputs to 32-bit values first
questions.explain: Division assumes x >= 0 and y > 0, so negative inputs are handled by dividing their absolute values and fixing the sign afterward. Multiplication is the operation that works as-is on two's complement values.

questions.q: Which properties of the square root function let it be computed with binary search?
choices: Its inverse function (x^2) can be computed efficiently
It is monotonically increasing
Its result is always even
It can be computed with a single bit shift
questions.explain: Monotonicity means you can test a candidate y and know which direction to search, and squaring makes each test cheap. Together these allow a binary search for y with y^2 <= x < (y+1)^2.

questions.q: sqrt(x) for 16-bit numbers sets y = 0, then for j = 7 down to 0: if (y + 2^j)^2 <= x then y = y + 2^j. Running sqrt(50), which values of j cause y to be updated?
questions.explain: For j = 7..3, (2^j)^2 is at least 64, which is more than 50, so y stays 0. j = 2: 16 <= 50, y = 4. j = 1: 6^2 = 36 <= 50, y = 6. j = 0: 7^2 = 49 <= 50, y = 7. The result is 7.

questions.q: In sqrt, computing (y + 2^j)^2 can overflow. How should the update condition be changed?
choices: Use: (y + 2^j)^2 < x and y < 0
Start j at n instead of n/2 - 1
Compare y + 2^j against x / 2 instead of squaring
questions.explain: An overflowed square wraps to a negative (or zero) value, which would wrongly pass the <= x test. Also requiring the square to be positive rejects those cases.

questions.q: Memory.init executes let ram = 0; where ram is a static Array. Why does this let peek and poke reach any RAM word?
choices: Accessing ram[addr] compiles to code that accesses address 0 + addr, which is RAM[addr]
Setting ram to 0 clears all of RAM so it can be reused
It points ram at the heap base address, 2048
It turns off array bounds checking in the compiler
questions.explain: Jack is weakly typed, so assigning 0 to an Array variable compiles without complaint. After that, ram[addr] is base 0 + addr, and peek and poke become one-liners on the ram array.

questions.q: A simple heap manager starts with heap = freeList = 2048. alloc(size) does block = freeList; freeList = freeList + size; return block. A program calls Memory.alloc(5), then Memory.alloc(4). What base address does the second call return?
questions.explain: The first call returns 2048 and moves freeList to 2053. The second call returns 2053 and moves freeList to 2057.

questions.q: In the simple heap manager (where alloc just advances freeList), deAlloc returns the block to the free list so it can be reused.
questions.explain: In the simple scheme deAlloc does nothing, so memory is never recycled. The real heap manager keeps a linked list of free segments to fix this.

questions.q: The freeList holds segments of sizes 4, 9, 6 and 12, in that order. A segment is 'possible' for alloc(size) if segment.size >= size + 2. For alloc(4), which segment does each heuristic choose?
choices: First fit: the 9-word segment; best fit: the 6-word segment
First fit: the 4-word segment; best fit: the 4-word segment
First fit: the 9-word segment; best fit: the 12-word segment
First fit: the 6-word segment; best fit: the 9-word segment
questions.explain: alloc(4) needs a segment of at least 6 words. First fit takes the first possible segment in list order (9). Best fit takes the smallest possible segment (6).

questions.q: For alloc(10), how many words does the linked-list heap manager carve out of the chosen segment?
questions.explain: It carves a block of size + 2 words. The 2 extra words are bookkeeping overhead (the next and size fields), and alloc returns the base address of the block's data part.

questions.q: In the linked-list heap manager, what does deAlloc(object) do?
choices: Appends the object's block to the end of the freeList
Immediately merges the block with adjacent free segments
Writes 0 into every word of the block
Nothing; memory is never recycled
questions.explain: deAlloc just appends the freed block to the freeList. Merging segments is a separate defragmentation step.

questions.q: What problem grows the more a program recycles memory with deAlloc, and what is the suggested fix?
choices: The freeList becomes fragmented into many small segments; periodically defragment it
The stack overflows into the heap; enlarge the stack
The freeList becomes circular; add a cycle-detection pass
Allocated blocks get overwritten; zero each block on alloc
questions.explain: Each deAlloc appends another (often small) segment, so the freeList becomes fragmented. Periodic defragmentation of the freeList fixes this.

questions.q: In the proposed Memory.init, heap = 2048 and the whole heap starts as one free segment: heap[0] = 0 (next) and heap[1] = its length. What length value is stored in heap[1]?
questions.explain: The heap runs from 2048 up to 16383 (the I/O memory maps start at 16384), which is 14336 words. Subtracting the 2 bookkeeping words leaves 14334.

questions.q: When Jack code creates an object with new, what code does the compiler generate to get memory for it?
choices: A call to Memory.alloc(n), where n is the size needed
A call to Array.new(n), which reserves space on the stack
A push onto the VM stack segment
A call to Memory.poke at the next free heap address
questions.explain: Object construction calls Memory.alloc(n) to get a heap block. Recycling an object's memory uses Memory.deAlloc(obj).

questions.q: drawPixel(x, y) computes address = 32*y + x/16 and modifies the word at RAM[16384 + address]. For drawPixel(100, 10), which RAM address is modified?
For drawPixel(100, 10), which bit of that 16-bit word is set to the current color?
questions.explain: The bit index is x % 16 = 100 % 16 = 4. Setting a single bit is done with 16-bit logical operations (AND/OR with a mask).

questions.q: Why does the drawPixel address formula multiply y by 32?
choices: Each 512-pixel screen row occupies 512 / 16 = 32 sixteen-bit words
The screen has 32 rows
Each character is 32 pixels wide
The screen memory map starts 32 words after 16384
questions.explain: The screen is 256 rows of 512 black-and-white pixels, and each RAM word holds 16 pixels, so one row takes 32 words.

questions.q: drawLine (for north-east lines) avoids computing the slope test b/a > dy/dx directly. What does it track instead?
choices: diff = a*dy - b*dx: if diff < 0 go right (a++, diff += dy), otherwise go up (b++, diff -= dx)
diff = a*dx - b*dy: if diff < 0 go up (b++), otherwise go right (a++)
The slope dy/dx, recomputed each step with Math.divide
The distance from the current pixel to the line, computed with Math.sqrt
questions.explain: b/a > dy/dx is equivalent to a*dy < b*dx, i.e. diff < 0. Each step changes diff by +dy or -dx, so drawLine needs only addition and subtraction.

questions.q: Tracing the optimized drawLine from (0,0) to (3,2) with a = b = diff = 0: after drawing the first pixel, which way does it move?
choices: Up (b++), because diff = 0 is not less than 0
Right (a++), because diff = 0
Diagonally (both a++ and b++)
Nowhere; the loop ends after one pixel
questions.explain: The rule is: if diff < 0 go right, otherwise go up. With diff = 0 it goes up, and diff becomes 0 - dx = -3.

questions.q: With dx = 3 and dy = 2, the loop runs while (a <= dx) and (b <= dy). How many pixels does drawLine draw in total?
questions.explain: Trace: (0,0) up, (0,1) right, (1,1) right, (2,1) up, (2,2) right, (3,2) up. Then b = 3 > dy and the loop ends after 6 pixels (dx + dy + 1).

questions.q: drawCircle(x, y, r) draws, for each dy from -r to r, a horizontal line from (x - sqrt(r^2 - dy^2), y + dy) to (x + sqrt(r^2 - dy^2), y + dy). For drawCircle(100, 100, 5) and dy = 3, which line is drawn?
questions.explain: sqrt(25 - 9) = sqrt(16) = 4, so the line spans x = 96..104 at y = 103. Stacking these lines produces a filled circle.

questions.q: Why is drawCircle's radius limited to r <= 181?
choices: Larger r makes r^2 overflow 16-bit arithmetic: 181^2 = 32761 fits, but 182^2 = 33124 > 32767
The screen is only 181 pixels tall
Math.sqrt only accepts arguments up to 181
drawLine cannot draw lines longer than 181 pixels
questions.explain: The algorithm computes r^2 - dy^2, and 181 is the largest r whose square fits in a signed 16-bit value.

questions.q: What distinguishes a vector graphics file from a bitmap graphics file?
choices: It stores drawing commands such as drawLine(3,0,11,0) and drawRectangle(3,1,9,5)
It stores the image as rows of 0/1 pixel values
It stores only the image's color palette
It stores a compressed copy of the screen memory map
questions.explain: A vector file is a list of drawing primitives, so it can easily be scaled, stored, transmitted and turned into a bitmap. A bitmap file lists pixel values row by row.

questions.q: On the Hack-Jack platform, graphics work like line drawing is offloaded from the CPU to a dedicated graphics processor (GPU).
questions.explain: Most modern computers use a GPU, but Hack-Jack has no such separation: the CPU runs the OS's Screen functions directly.

questions.q: Each Hack font character occupies a frame 8 pixels wide. How many character columns fit across the 512-pixel-wide screen?
questions.explain: 512 / 8 = 64. This is how Output turns the 256 x 512 pixel grid into a 23 x 64 character grid.

questions.q: Each Hack font character frame is 11 pixels high. How many full text rows fit on the 256-pixel-tall screen?
questions.explain: 256 / 11 = 23.27, so 23 full rows fit (rows 0..22).

questions.q: Each 11 x 8 Hack font frame contains 2 empty right columns and 1 empty bottom row. What are they for?
choices: Spacing between adjacent characters
Room to draw the cursor
Storing the character's code
Parity bits for error detection
questions.explain: The empty columns and bottom row keep neighboring characters from touching. Another row is kept for 'squiggles' that dip below the line, as in Q.

questions.q: In calls like Output.create(0, 63,63,63,63,63,63,63,63,63,0,0), each argument after the index is one row of the bitmap. Why is 63 the largest row value?
choices: Only 6 of a row's 8 pixel columns are ever drawn (the 2 right columns are spacing), and 6 bits max out at 63
Characters are 6 pixels high
The Hack character set has 63 printable characters
63 is the code for '?', which marks unknown characters
questions.explain: 63 = 111111 in binary, which is all 6 drawable pixels on. This call builds the solid black square used for non-printable characters.

questions.q: How many row values does Output.create take to define one character's bitmap (not counting the character index)?
questions.explain: Each character is 11 pixels high, so its bitmap is an 11-element array, stored in the static charMaps array at the character's index.

questions.q: When Output prints the backspace character, what happens to the cursor?
choices: It moves one column left
It moves to the beginning of the next line
A black square is displayed and the cursor moves right
It stays where it is
questions.explain: newLine moves the cursor to the start of the next line, and backspace moves it one column left. Any other character has its bitmap displayed, and the cursor moves one column right.

questions.q: In the Hack character set, '0' has code 48 and the digits are consecutive. What is the code for '7'?
questions.explain: 48 + 7 = 55. The same fact converts a digit character to its integer value: subtract 48.

questions.q: What is the Hack character code for newline?
questions.explain: The non-printable keys start at 128: newline 128, backspace 129, then the arrow keys (left 130, up 131, right 132, down 133), and so on.

questions.q: Output.moveCursor(i, j) moves the cursor to row j, column i.
questions.explain: It moves the cursor to the j'th column of the i'th row, and erases the character that was there.

questions.q: At what RAM address is the Hack keyboard memory map (a single 16-bit register)?
questions.explain: The screen memory map takes 16384..24575, and the one-word keyboard map comes right after it at 24576.

questions.q: RAM[24576] holds 0000000000110100. Which key is being pressed?
questions.explain: 110100 in binary is 32 + 16 + 4 = 52, which is the Hack code for the digit '4'.

questions.q: What does Keyboard.keyPressed() return when no key is being pressed?
choices: Nothing; it waits until a key is pressed
questions.explain: keyPressed doesn't wait. It reads the keyboard register (e.g. with Memory.peek(24576)), which holds 0 when no key is down.

questions.q: Which sequence matches Keyboard.readChar()?
choices: Display the cursor; wait until a key is pressed; record its code c; wait until the key is released; display c and advance the cursor; return c
Wait until a key is pressed; return its code c immediately, then display it
Display the cursor; wait until a key is released; then wait until a key is pressed; return c without echoing it
Read keyPressed() once; if it is nonzero, display it; return it
questions.explain: readChar busy-waits while keyPressed() == 0, records c, and then busy-waits while keyPressed() != 0. Only after the key is released does it echo c and advance the cursor.

questions.q: During Keyboard.readLine, the user types c, a, t, backspace, r, newline. What string is returned?
questions.explain: readLine appends ordinary characters. On backspace it removes the last character from str and calls Output.backSpace. On newline it displays the newline and returns str. So the result is 'cat' minus 't' plus 'r' = 'car'.

questions.q: Keyboard.readInt(message) reads a line and returns its integer value up to the first non-numeric character. If the user types 1, 2, x, 5, newline, what is returned?
questions.explain: The digits 1 and 2 build the value 12. Parsing stops at 'x', so the 5 is ignored.

questions.q: How should Keyboard.keyPressed be implemented?
choices: Use Memory.peek to read the keyboard memory map
Call readChar and throw away the echoed character
Ask Output for the last character it printed
Use Memory.poke to request a key from the keyboard
questions.explain: The keyboard register at RAM[24576] always holds the code of the key currently pressed (or 0), so a single Memory.peek is all keyPressed needs.

questions.q: let s = String.new(10); then s = s.appendChar(97); s = s.appendChar(98); s = s.appendChar(99). What does s.length() return?
questions.explain: new(maxLength) sets the maximum capacity, but length() returns the actual length: 3 characters, 'abc'.

questions.q: A String s holds "42ab7". What does s.intValue() return?
questions.explain: intValue returns the integer value of the string up to the first non-numeric character, so parsing stops at 'a'.

questions.q: string2Int sets val = 0, then for each character does val = val * 10 + d, where d is that digit's integer value. For the string "4072", what is val after the first three characters?
questions.explain: 0*10 + 4 = 4, then 4*10 + 0 = 40, then 40*10 + 7 = 407. (After the last character it is 4072.)

questions.q: Which describes the int2String(val) algorithm from the slides (used by String.setInt)?
choices: Recursive: if val < 10, return the digit character as a string; otherwise return int2String(val / 10) with the character for val % 10 appended
Iterative: repeatedly append val % 10 to an empty string, then reverse the string
Look up val in a precomputed table of digit strings
Repeatedly subtract powers of 10 from val, counting each subtraction
questions.explain: The recursion converts the higher digits first and then appends the last digit, so the digits come out in the right order without a reversal step.

questions.q: What do String.newLine(), String.backSpace() and String.doubleQuote() return, respectively?
questions.explain: These are the Hack character codes: newline = 128, backspace = 129, double quote = 34.

questions.q: In the OS Array class, new(size) must be implemented as a function, not as a constructor.
questions.explain: Array.new is declared as a function that returns an Array. Its counterpart, dispose, is implemented with Memory.deAlloc.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly describes how a Jack program gets started (bootstrapping)?
choices: On reset the computer executes ROM[0]; that code sets SP = 256 and calls Sys.init; Sys.init initializes the OS classes and calls Main.main()
On reset Main.main() runs first, and it calls Sys.init when it needs OS services
Sys.init sets SP = 256, then the hardware jumps to ROM[0], which calls Main.main()
The VM places Main.main() at ROM[0], and Sys.init runs only after Main.main() returns
questions.explain: Hardware contract: reset runs ROM[0]. VM contract: the code at ROM[0] sets SP = 256 and calls Sys.init. OS contract: Sys.init initializes the OS and calls Main.main(). Jack contract: execution starts at Main.main().

questions.q: Sys.init calls the init functions of Memory, Math, Screen, Output and Keyboard, then Main.main(). What does it call after Main.main() returns?
choices: Sys.halt()
Main.main() again
Sys.error(0)
Nothing; control returns to ROM[0]
questions.explain: Sys.init ends with Sys.halt(), which is implemented as an infinite loop, so the machine stops doing useful work once the program finishes.

questions.q: Sys.error(errorCode) prints the code in the format ERR<errorCode> and then returns to the caller.
questions.explain: Sys.error prints ERR<errorCode> and then halts. It does not return.
